amendments.rule: The **substantival article** — `הַ` on a participle or adjective used as a noun — takes the pronoun the ASV supplies to make it substantival, and heads on that pronoun rather than on the relative that follows it. `הָרַע` → *that which was evil* is the article with *that which*, headed on *that*; `הָעֹשֶׂה` → *him that doeth* is the article with *him that*, headed on *him*. The supplied pronoun is the article's own rendering and is never `added`. The predicate word keeps its own English, including any copula the ASV supplies, which stays with it under rule 20: in *that which is right*, *is* and *right* belong to the adjective and only *that which* belongs to the article. **An attributive article the ASV renders by a relative goes the same way.** Where `הַ` stands on a participle or adjective modifying an explicit noun and the ASV writes a relative instead of a *the* — `אֹיְבֶיךָ הַקָּמִים עָלֶיךָ` → *thine enemies that rise up against thee*, `הָאִישׁ הָרַךְ` → *The man that is tender*, `הַכְּתוּבִים` → *that are written*, `הַכֹּהֵן הַמְחַטֵּא` → *The priest that offereth* — the article takes that relative and heads on it, while the participle or adjective keeps its own English together with any supplied copula, exactly as above. **But read where the ASV has put the attributive before reaching for that sentence.** Where it renders the attributive prenominally instead, no relative stands before the attributive's own word and rule 47 governs the count: the phrase's single *the* is the first article's and the agreement article is `unrepresented`, as `הַכֹּהֵן הַמָּשִׁיחַ` → *the anointed priest* is. **A demonstrative, possessive or quantifying determiner the ASV writes in the article's place goes the same way, whatever the article stands on.** Where the ASV writes no *the* for the phrase but a *this*, *that*, *these*, *those*, a possessive *his*, *her*, *thy*, *thine*, or a quantifier such as *any* or *every*, standing where the phrase's *the* would stand — `הַזִּמָּה` → *this lewdness*, `הַגְּדֹלוֹת` → *thine elder*, `הַבֶּגֶד` → *any garment* — that word is what the ASV has written for the article: the article takes it and heads on it, and it is neither `added` nor a reason to mark the article `unrepresented`. A quantifying determiner is read on exactly the terms of the others and is not left to the noun under rule 15: that rule gives a supplied *any* to the nominal expression only where no determiner morpheme stands before the word it determines, and an article standing on that word is such a morpheme. **Read that as no *the* standing before the article's own word, not as no *the* anywhere in the phrase.** Where the article sits on the *nomen rectum* of a construct chain and the ASV writes a *the* before the construct and a demonstrative or possessive before the rectum's own word, rule 29's arthrous case governs the count: nothing is fronted, the article takes the determiner standing before its own word, and the construct takes the supplied *the*. `יְמֵי הַמִּשְׁתֶּה` → *the days of* ***their*** *feasting* gives *their* to the article and *the days* to the construct, exactly as `שְׂדֵה הָעִיר` → *the fields of the city* gives the second *the* to the article there. Do not mark such an article `unrepresented` and the determiner `added` under rule 18's closing sentence: that sentence governs a supplied possessive with no determiner morpheme standing before the word it determines, and here one does. **But only where no other morpheme licenses that determiner.** A pronominal suffix standing in the same phrase is rendered by a possessive of its own under rule 18, a `כֹּל` standing on the noun is itself what an *any* or an *every* renders under rule 15, an `אֶחָד` standing in the phrase is itself what a distributive *each* or *every* renders, and a demonstrative pronoun standing in the phrase is itself what a written *this*, *that*, *these* or *those* renders; where the ASV writes one determiner for the whole phrase that morpheme takes it and the article is `unrepresented`: `אֲחוֹתֵךְ הַגְּדוֹלָה` → *thine elder sister* gives *thine* to the suffix on `אָחוֹת` and leaves the article nothing, while `אֲחוֹתַיִךְ הַגְּדֹלוֹת` → *thy sisters, thine elder sisters* writes a determiner for each and the article takes the second; so too `אֲחִיהֶם הַבְּכוֹר` → *their eldest brother's*, where the suffix takes *their* and the article has nothing, and `הַמָּקוֹם הַהוּא` → *that place*, where `הוּא` takes the written *that* while the noun's article and the agreement article beside it are both `unrepresented` under rule 47. **And the morpheme that licenses the determiner need not stand inside the noun phrase.** What the preceding sentences ask is which morpheme the written determiner answers to, so read the clause rather than the phrase's edges: where a dative or possessive `לְ` with a pronominal suffix stands beside the noun and the ASV recasts it as a possessive determiner on that noun, the suffix is what the determiner realizes under rules 18 and 40, the `לְ` is `unrepresented` under rule 40, and the article is `unrepresented` exactly as it is beside a suffix written on the noun itself. `וַיְהִי לָהֶם הַגְּבוּל` → *And* ***their*** *border was* gives *their* to the suffix, *was* to `הָיָה` under rule 43, and nothing to either the preposition or the article. Do not hand such a determiner to the article on the ground that the suffix stands outside the phrase: that would leave the morpheme the ASV wrote the word for holding nothing, against rules 2 and 18. Count the determiners and read which word each stands before, as rule 29 counts the ASV's *the*s. **The `אֶחָד` case is counted on exactly those terms, and it turns on the one word the ASV wrote rather than on where that word stands.** A distributive determiner stands precisely where the phrase's *the* would stand, so the preceding sentences alone would hand it to the article; the numeral takes it because the numeral is itself what the word says. Where the ASV writes one such determiner, it is the numeral's and every article in the phrase — the noun's own and the agreement article on the numeral alike — is `unrepresented`: `לַפָּר הָאֶחָד` → *for* ***each*** *bullock* and `לַכֶּבֶשׂ הָאֶחָד` → *for* ***every*** *lamb*. Where it instead writes a *the* before the noun and an *one* for the numeral, two determiners are written and each morpheme takes the one standing before its own word: `לָאַיִל הָאֶחָד` → *for* ***the one*** *ram* gives *the* to the noun's article and *one* to the numeral, the agreement article still `unrepresented` under rule 47. One verse may write both shapes, and NUM.28.12 and NUM.28.28 do. The corpus aligns `אֶחָד` to *each* in 18 units, to *every* in four and to *every one* in five, so a numeral standing in the phrase is a morpheme that licenses such a determiner; the article's own units of *every* are the case this sentence excludes, where no such numeral stands. **And a determiner another morpheme licenses is still a determiner standing before the article's own word.** The count above is unchanged where the preceding sentences have left the article with nothing: still nothing is fronted, and where such a phrase is the *nomen rectum* of a construct chain the construct takes a supplied *the* of its own. `שֵׁם הַמָּקוֹם הַהוּא` → *the name of that place* gives *the name* to the construct, *that* to the demonstrative pronoun, and nothing to either article. Do not read the article's silence as an anarthrous rendering and hand the construct's *the* back to it as a fronted determiner: what forces fronting under rule 29 is a rectum the ASV renders with no determiner at all — `לֻחֹת הָאֲבָנִים` → *the two tables of stone* — and a rectum whose own word carries a *this*, a *that* or a possessive is not that, whichever morpheme in the phrase the word answers to. Read what stands before the rectum's word, not which morpheme was left with nothing. Read what the ASV writes for the article and let that decide which rule governs: a bare *the* is rule 15's ordinary attributive article, a relative or a supplied pronoun is this rule's, a demonstrative, possessive or quantifying determiner is this rule's too, and where the ASV writes none of them the article is `unrepresented` under rule 29. Where coordinated attributives share a single written relative, the first article takes it and the rest are `unrepresented` under rules 22 and 47. **An articleless attributive that the ASV recasts as a relative clause keeps the supplied relative with the attributive itself.** Where an adjective or participle without an article modifies an explicit noun and the ASV writes a relative frame — `אֲדָמָה טְמֵאָה` → *a land that is unclean* — the attributive takes the relative together with its own English and any copula rule 20 supplies, headed on the word carrying its lexeme. The relative realizes the Hebrew attributive relation and is not `added`; rule 55's supplied clause subordinator is a different construction.
amendments.why: Rule 41's carve-out for a determiner another morpheme licenses names 'a pronominal suffix standing in the same phrase'. Its governing sentence — 'only where no other morpheme licenses that determiner' — is general, but the example wording reads as the condition, and JOS.13.16 and JOS.13.25 are the case it does not literally reach: the suffix that *their* realizes stands on לָהֶם, outside the noun phrase הַגְּבוּל, while the article sits inside it. Rule 40 already rules that a dative לְ recast as a possessive determiner leaves the preposition unrepresented and gives the pronoun to the suffix (לְרַע לוֹ → *to his hurt*), so the licensing morpheme is settled; what was missing was the statement that rule 41's count reads the clause and not the phrase boundary. Without it a verse pass can give *their* to the article and leave the suffix holding nothing, which rules 2 and 18 forbid. The added sentences change no existing ruling and are placed beside the examples they qualify; the rest of the rule, including the אֶחָד count, the fronting limit and the articleless-attributive paragraph, is returned unchanged. The construction is the Joshua allotment formula and recurs through the remaining tribal chapters.

conventions: Construct chain whose nomen rectum is a toponym carrying an article: count the ASV's *the*s for the whole phrase before placing them, and do not read the toponym's article as lexicalized in the name. Where a single *the* is written, it is that article's and the construct noun stands bare — אַשְׁדּוֹת הַפִּסְגָּה → *the slopes of Pisgah* (13.20), שֵׁבֶט הַלֵּוִי → *the tribe of Levi* (13.14, 13.33), חֲצִי הַשֵּׁבֶט → *the half tribe* (13.7), עָרֵי הַגִּלְעָד → *the cities of Gilead* (13.25). Where the ASV writes no *the* for the phrase at all, the article is `unrepresented` and nothing is supplied on the construct — *all Bashan* (13.11, 13.30), *half Gilead* (13.31), *king of Bashan* (13.30), *Ramath mizpeh* (13.26), *from Lebanon* (13.6). Where two *the*s are written, each morpheme takes the one standing before its own word — *the border of the Geshurites* (13.11), *the cities of the plain* (13.21), *the remnant of the Rephaim* (13.12). What decides which case a phrase is, is whether a *the* is written for the phrase, not whether one stands before the toponym's own word.

The allotment formula וַיְהִי לָ+suffix הַגְּבוּל → *And their border was* divides four ways, and the same division holds wherever it recurs: הָיָה takes the copula (rule 43), the suffix takes the possessive *their* (rules 18, 40), the לְ is `unrepresented` because the ASV spends no word on its relation (rule 40), and the noun's own article is `unrepresented` because the possessive is the phrase's one written determiner and the suffix, not the article, is what licenses it (rule 41). JOS.13.16 and JOS.13.25 are the formula with the preposition; JOS.13.30 writes גְבוּלָם with the suffix on the noun itself and divides identically apart from having no לְ to silence.

The corpus aligns `אֶחָד` to *each* in 18 units, to *every* in four and to *every one* in five, so a numeral standing in the phrase is a morpheme that licenses such a determiner; the article's own units of *every* are the case this sentence excludes, where no such numeral stands. **And a determiner another morpheme licenses is still a determiner standing before the article's own word.** The count above is unchanged where the preceding sentences have left the article with nothing: still nothing is fronted, and where such a phrase is the *nomen rectum* of a construct chain the construct takes a supplied *the* of its own. `שֵׁם הַמָּקוֹם הַהוּא` → *the name of that place* gives *the name* to the construct, *that* to the demonstrative pronoun, and nothing to either article. Do not read the article's silence as an anarthrous rendering and hand the construct's *the* back to it as a fronted determiner: what forces fronting under rule 29 is a rectum the ASV renders with no determiner at all — `לֻחֹת הָאֲבָנִים` → *the two tables of stone* — and a rectum whose own word carries a *this*, a *that* or a possessive is not that, whichever morpheme in the phrase the word answers to. Read what stands before the rectum's word, not which morpheme was left with nothing. Read what the ASV writes for the article and let that decide which rule governs: a bare *the* is rule 15's ordinary attributive article, a relative or a supplied pronoun is this rule's, a demonstrative, possessive or quantifying determiner is this rule's too, and where the ASV writes none of them the article is `unrepresented` under rule 29. Where coordinated attributives share a single written relative, the first article takes it and the rest are `unrepresented` under rules 22 and 47. **An articleless attributive that the ASV recasts as a relative clause keeps the supplied relative with the attributive itself.** Where an adjective or participle without an article modifies an explicit noun and the ASV writes a relative frame — `אֲדָמָה טְמֵאָה` → *a land that is unclean* — the attributive takes the relative together with its own English and any copula rule 20 supplies, headed on the word carrying its lexeme. The relative realizes the Hebrew attributive relation and is not `added`; rule 55's supplied clause subordinator is a different construction.
amended.why: Rule 41's carve-out for a determiner another morpheme licenses names 'a pronominal suffix standing in the same phrase'. Its governing sentence — 'only where no other morpheme licenses that determiner' — is general, but the example wording reads as the condition, and JOS.13.16 and JOS.13.25 are the case it does not literally reach: the suffix that *their* realizes stands on לָהֶם, outside the noun phrase הַגְּבוּל, while the article sits inside it. Rule 40 already rules that a dative לְ recast as a possessive determiner leaves the preposition unrepresented and gives the pronoun to the suffix (לְרַע לוֹ → *to his hurt*), so the licensing morpheme is settled; what was missing was the statement that rule 41's count reads the clause and not the phrase boundary. Without it a verse pass can give *their* to the article and leave the suffix holding nothing, which rules 2 and 18 forbid. The added sentences change no existing ruling and are placed beside the examples they qualify; the rest of the rule, including the אֶחָד count, the fronting limit and the articleless-attributive paragraph, is returned unchanged. The construction is the Joshua allotment formula and recurs through the remaining tribal chapters.

report: One real cross-verse split, in JOS.13.25. A construct chain whose nomen rectum is a toponym carrying an article, with a single written *the*, is analysed one way at JOS.13.7, 13.14, 13.20 and 13.33 — the article takes the written *the*, fronted to the phrase's left edge, and the construct stands bare — and the opposite way at JOS.13.25 (עָרֵי הַגִּלְעָד → *the cities of Gilead*), where the construct was given a supplied *the* and the article was marked unrepresented. Rule 29's toponym paragraph settles it; JOS.13.25 is patched.

The verse note that produced the error read 'No *the* written before Gilead', which is true of JOS.13.11 and JOS.13.31 (*and Gilead*, *half Gilead*, no *the* anywhere in the phrase, article rightly unrepresented) but not of JOS.13.25, where a *the* is written and some morpheme must carry it. The operative test is whether the ASV writes a *the* for the phrase at all, not whether one stands before the toponym's own word.

Everything else in the 52-lemma table is licensed by context. The preposition-plus-construct-noun pairs divide exactly on rule 30's one-rendering condition: bə + tôḵ → *in the middle* (13.9, 13.16), bə + qereb → *in the midst* (13.13) and min + pənê → *from before* (13.6) split because a word is written for each, while bə + ʿēber (13.8), mē + ʿēber (13.32) and ʿal + pənê (13.3, 13.25) fuse; the bare ʿēber of 13.27 carries *beyond* alone because no preposition stands there.

The four dispositions of *even* each follow rule 16's count of connective morphemes: to the waw at 13.3, whole inside kaʾăšer → *even as* at 13.8, and `added` at 13.6 and 13.31 where no waw and no object marker stands before the phrase it introduces. The lə + 3mp suffix units divide on whether the ASV spends a word on the relation — aligned *unto them* at 13.33, unrepresented at 13.8, 13.16, 13.25 and 13.32 where the recasting leaves it nothing.

The two supplied nouns that look like a pair are not one: the italic *inheritance* at 13.29 is `added` because nātan's own English has already written its lexeme (rule 44), while *the inheritances* at 13.32 is the supplied antecedent of a written ʾăšer and joins that relative's unit (rule 46's first rider). Both verses name the competing reading in their notes, so no patch.

BSB: no genuine error among the disagreements. The 18 Td rows, the 4 R rows and the 2 ʾēt rows are the documented convention difference; the Sd rows at 13.4 and 13.18 are rule 32 working as written, since ʿad has already taken the directional word and the 13.18 name list writes none; hûʾ at 13.14 is the tripartite resumptive of rule 20. The 13.25 patch happens to move one Td toward BSB, but it is made on rule 29 and not on the aggregate.

Two conventions recorded (the toponym-rectum *the* count, and the four-way division of the allotment formula wayhî lāhem haggəbûl). One amendment, to rule 41: its carve-out names 'a pronominal suffix standing in the same phrase', and twice here (13.16, 13.25) the suffix licensing the written *their* stands on lāhem, outside the noun phrase. The governing sentence is already general; the example wording is not.
